newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, U.S. to seek speedy reporting of mishaps.
newsitem.headline: Japan, U.S. to seek speedy reporting of mishaps.

text.p: The United States and Japan said on Thursday they would try to thrash out a joint scheme to exchange information quickly on accidents involving U.S. military forces here.
The agreement came after a bomb was jettisoned by a U.S. military aircraft last week into Japanese waters off the southernmost island of Okinawa.

The two governments "will review notification procedures of such an incident so that relevant, timely information is transmitted to all applicable authorities," the U.S.-Japan Joint Committee said in a statement.
The committee comprises officials from the foreign and defence ministries of the two countries.
Although the bomb jettisoned by a U.S. Marine Corps jet fell harmlessly into the sea, a controversy flared over the way the U.S. military and Japanese authorities responded to the incident.

It took the U.S. military six hours to notify the Japanese Foreign Ministry of the incident and the ministry did not immediately report it to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, saying later that the report had been unconfirmed at that time.

The Japanese coastguard waited a full 24 hours after the jettisoning to seal off the area to inter-island ferries. There was a chance that the bomb could have exploded if passing ships caused a change in the surrounding water pressure.
Okinawa houses more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan, a legacy of the U.S. Occupation which followed a bloody World War Two battle there in 1945.
A public outcry against the huge U.S. military presence on the island erupted last year after the rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
Japan and the United States agreed in early December on a plan to streamline U.S. bases on Okinawa but without reducing the 28,000 U.S. military personnel stationed there.
